target: AG1’s claim that making Election Day a national holiday would remove scheduling barriers and make voting easier for everyone
objection: A federal holiday does not automatically give private-sector workers paid time off, so many low-income hourly workers in retail, restaurants, caregiving, and similar jobs could still be required to work and might not benefit from the holiday at all.

target: AG1’s broader assumption that a holiday is an effective turnout policy on its own
objection: Research and policy experience suggest that an election-day holiday by itself is not a reliable way to increase turnout compared with targeted voting-access reforms such as guaranteed time off to vote, automatic voter registration, and expanded early voting or vote-by-mail.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday is only a standalone symbol and does not solve the problem
objection: The holiday is not meant to stand alone; it can be paired with rules guaranteeing time off to vote. The complaint about private employers is therefore an implementation issue, not a reason to reject the holiday itself.

target: AG2’s argument that federal holiday status will not help because many workers would still work
objection: Even if some people still work, a holiday can improve conditions by increasing the pool of poll workers and helping facilities operate with more staffing, which can reduce lines and access problems.

target: AG1’s reply that the holiday can be paired with other reforms, especially guaranteed time off to vote
objection: If the holiday only works when additional work-time guarantees are added, then the holiday itself is not the main solution; it becomes a detour that could distract from or delay the direct employer-access rules that actually help hourly workers.

target: AG1’s suggestion that a stacked package of holiday plus other reforms is enough
objection: Even in a combined package, federal holiday status still does not automatically change private employers’ staffing decisions in retail and service jobs, so low-income workers may still face the same work pressures while businesses and public-sector operations absorb the costs.

target: AG1’s claim that adding more poll workers and improving facilities through a holiday meaningfully helps turnout
objection: Those staffing benefits are only incremental and do not substitute for the core access question of whether voters can actually get time off, find a polling place, and navigate registration and other voting logistics.

target: AG2’s renewed claim that the holiday mainly repeats the point that it is not sufficient by itself
objection: A national holiday would standardize access nationwide and reduce the patchwork of state-by-state and sector-by-sector compliance, making it easier for people to plan time off to vote.

target: AG2’s focus on work schedules to the exclusion of other barriers
objection: A holiday also reduces school and childcare logistics, which are separate and important scheduling barriers for voters, especially parents whose difficulty is not just getting time off from work.

target: AG1’s idea that a holiday naturally reduces childcare barriers
objection: Closing schools and daycares does not guarantee substitute childcare; for low-income parents it may instead create lost wages or unexpected childcare costs, so the holiday can fail to reduce and can even worsen the constraint.

target: AG1’s claim that nationwide standardization solves the access problem
objection: A national holiday still does not create an enforceable right to time off from the jobs that matter, while targeted employer time-off or paid-leave rules are what actually change behavior in retail and service sectors.

target: AG1’s argument that the holiday’s incremental gains justify it
objection: If the holiday only matters when combined with other reforms, then it is at best an add-on with weaker and less predictable effects, and it may crowd out or delay the more direct reforms that address the real bottlenecks.

target: AG2’s renewed claim that the holiday does not reliably change the work/school/childcare conflict
objection: Voting does not require a whole day off; a holiday changes the default schedule and gives parents and workers flexibility to vote during polling hours without taking additional time away from employment.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday is not enforceable enough to matter
objection: A holiday changes employer defaults and can be paired with clear federal time-to-vote requirements, so the policy is not merely symbolic and does not rely on vague voluntary compliance.

target: AG1’s reliance on the idea that a holiday automatically gives low-income workers paid or guaranteed time to vote
objection: Even on Election Day as a holiday, essential and customer-facing workplaces often stay open and staff on rotation, so many low-wage workers can still be scheduled to work unless there is an enforceable right to time to vote.

target: AG2’s claim that holiday status alone is too weak to justify the policy
objection: International precedent and bipartisan support show that the policy is workable and broadly acceptable: many OECD countries hold elections on weekends or holidays, and there is substantial public support in both parties.

target: AG1’s use of polling support and OECD precedent as evidence for the policy
objection: Those facts do not prove effectiveness in the United States, because other OECD countries may have different labor laws and election systems, and public support does not show that the policy actually changes turnout or private-employer scheduling incentives.

target: AG1’s argument that a holiday remains useful even when paired with enforceable time-to-vote protections
objection: If enforceable time-to-vote protections are added anyway, the holiday becomes largely redundant because the operative fix is the worker-right to time off, not the calendar designation.

target: AG2’s claim that the holiday is redundant if time-to-vote protections exist
objection: A holiday reduces the need for workers to know, request, or negotiate time off, thereby lowering uncertainty and the burden of bargaining with employers even when legal time-to-vote rights exist.

target: AG2’s claim that early voting and vote-by-mail can replace a holiday
objection: Early voting does not eliminate last-minute decision-day and coordination problems for people who cannot plan weeks ahead and need one shared national voting day for family and community planning.

target: AG1’s view that a holiday plus other measures is the right package
objection: Once enforceable time-to-vote protections are required for the policy to work, the holiday is an uncertain add-on rather than the best tool, and it may also reduce access to support services like transit or customer-service capacity on a public holiday.

target: AG2’s concern that holiday-related service disruptions could hurt voters
objection: Election Day is a government-administered event, so election-critical services can be kept open and planned for; unlike a generic holiday, polling places, assistance, and accessibility supports can be maintained or expanded.

target: AG1’s claim that election services can remain open and that the main barrier is still scheduling
objection: Keeping election services open does not solve the problem of whether low-income workers can afford to vote, because a holiday is time off in name only if employers do not grant paid leave and workers lose wages needed for transport, childcare, or other costs.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday can be written into law to trigger predictable time off
objection: That concedes the real mechanism is the enforceable worker-right, not the holiday itself; if the bill must already guarantee paid or allowed time to vote, then the holiday is just redundant overhead that adds costs and political complexity.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday reduces day-of congestion and time-squeeze beyond legal time off
objection: If congestion and schedule pressure are the problem, longer early-voting periods or vote-by-mail solve it more directly than a single national holiday, which may even encourage people to wait for Election Day instead of using more flexible options.

target: AG1’s claim that broad support and international precedent show the holiday is workable
objection: Feasibility and popularity do not prove causal effectiveness, especially when the policy still may not change private-employer incentives without specific, enforceable time-to-vote rules.
